stories.headline: Wall Street slips back from its record as bond yields swing and stocks fall worldwide
stories.dek: The S&P 500 dipped 0.2% a day after its first record since August; France’s market fell 1.2% on debt worries.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday (Oct. 7) U.S. stocks took a small step back. The S&P 500, the big list of 500 U.S. companies, slipped 0.2%, one day after hitting an all-time high. The Dow fell 341 points (0.7%) and the Nasdaq slipped 0.2%. The main reason: bond yields jumped around. The 10-year Treasury yield, the interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow for 10 years, climbed as high as 5.36% in the morning, near its highest since 2002, before easing back to 5.28% after a big government bond sale went smoothly. Simple rule: when safe bonds pay more, stocks look less attractive, and loans get pricier for everyone. Oil also swung. Brent crude topped $102 a barrel, then settled at $100.20. Before the war with Iran it was about $72. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 index dropped 1.2%, one of the world’s biggest losses, because investors worry about France’s debt and budget.
stories.why_it_matters: Mortgage, car-loan and credit-card rates follow these bond yields. When yields stay above 5%, families and small businesses pay more to borrow, even while stock prices sit near records. Companies now have to deliver big profit growth to keep stocks up.
stories.camps: Calm view: a 0.2% dip after a record is normal, and the bond sale showed buyers still want U.S. debt. Worried view: governments in the U.S. and Europe keep borrowing more every day, the IMF says “very tough political choices” are coming, and oil prices depend on a war nobody can predict. If company profits disappoint, high yields could hit stocks hard.
stories.image_alt: A general view of the New York Stock Exchange in New York.

terms.explain: An index tracking 500 big U.S. companies; the most-watched measure of the U.S. stock market.
The interest the U.S. government pays to borrow money. Many other loan rates follow it.
The main world price for oil.
France’s main stock index, tracking 40 big French companies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, an index of 30 big U.S. companies.

stories.headline: Fed notes show most officials expect another interest-rate hike this year
stories.dek: Inflation is “still elevated,” the minutes say; traders expect no move in late October but a hike in December.
stories.caveman: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is America’s central bank. It raises interest rates to slow the economy when prices climb too fast. On Wednesday it released the “minutes,” the written notes, from its Sept. 15-16 meeting. At that meeting the Fed raised its key rate by a quarter point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years. The notes say officials all agreed inflation is still too high and has made little progress toward their 2% goal. Most of them expect another hike will likely be needed this year. Several said today’s rate is too low to really cool the economy, a hint they could back more than one more hike. Why are prices sticky? Oil and gas are expensive because of the Iran war, tariffs still push up costs, and AI demand is making chips, computer parts and electrical gear pricier. The Fed’s preferred inflation measure was 3.4% in August. Wall Street now bets the Fed will hold rates at its Oct. 28-29 meeting and raise them in December.
stories.why_it_matters: A higher Fed rate makes credit cards, car loans and business loans cost more. It is meant to cool spending so prices calm down, but it can also slow hiring. Many Americans are already struggling with high living costs.
stories.camps: Fed view: Chairman Kevin Warsh said “inflation is too high and has been for too long,” so they must act. Other officials, like vice chair Philip Jefferson, say they can take time to watch the effect of the last hike. President Trump has repeatedly called for rate cuts and criticized the Fed’s rate committee, though he still says he supports Warsh, whom he appointed. Critics of hikes worry about pushing the economy into a slowdown.
stories.image_alt: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a news conference in Washington on Sept. 16, 2026.

terms.explain: The central bank of the United States. It sets key interest rates.
The official written notes of what was said at a meeting.
When a central bank raises the cost of borrowing money.
When prices for everyday things keep rising over time.
Taxes on goods brought in from other countries.

stories.headline: IMF chief warns countries: cut your debt and get ready for AI, because a “far-reaching shock” is possible
stories.dek: Kristalina Georgieva says the world faces a triple hit from AI, heavy borrowing and wars, ahead of big meetings in Bangkok next week.
stories.caveman: The IMF (International Monetary Fund) is like a global money doctor for 191 countries. Its boss, Kristalina Georgieva, gave a speech in Singapore on Wednesday. Her message: “Some very tough political choices stare us in the face.” She said countries rich and poor must act faster to cut debt and fight growing inequality. Rich countries like the U.S., Japan and Germany carry big debts. Poor countries must choose between paying for schools and hospitals or paying back expensive loans while interest rates are high. She also talked about AI. Companies are spending so much building data centers that it may beat what the world once spent on railroads, power grids and phone networks. That spending lifts stock prices and growth, but it also pushes up inflation, and the benefits come later. “Should earnings fall short,” she warned, big tech borrowing and huge holdings of U.S. stocks “could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock.” “Love it, hate it or fear it, AI is here,” she said.
stories.why_it_matters: Finance ministers and central bankers meet in Bangkok next week at the IMF-World Bank meetings. What they decide about debt and rates affects jobs, prices and public services everywhere, including Asia, which now makes 43% of world economic activity.
stories.camps: Georgieva’s side: governments have the tools, and delaying action only makes the bill bigger. Pushback often heard: cutting debt usually means spending cuts or tax rises, which can hurt poor and working people first; many countries say their debts grew because of wars, the pandemic and high energy prices they did not cause. AI supporters argue the boom will pay for itself through higher productivity.
stories.image_alt: The International Monetary Fund logo on its building in Washington.

terms.explain: International Monetary Fund, a group of 191 countries that lends money and gives economic advice.
Money a government or person has borrowed and must pay back.
A growing gap between rich and poor people.
A huge building full of computers; AI needs many of them.
An international bank that lends to poorer countries for development projects.

stories.headline: Iraq makes its money cheaper as the Iran war chokes its oil shipping route
stories.dek: The official rate moved from about 1,300 to 1,500 dinars per dollar; street rates jumped past 1,700 and some exchange shops shut.
stories.caveman: Iraq earns most of its money by selling oil. Before the U.S. war with Iran, most of that oil sailed out through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea passage. The war has disrupted it, so Iraq now sends oil overland through Syria, which costs more and works less well. On Wednesday Iraq’s central bank “devalued” the dinar, its money. The official rate went from about 1,300 dinars for one U.S. dollar to 1,500. Simple idea: each oil dollar now turns into more dinars, which helps the government pay salaries and bills at home. But imported goods get more expensive. On the street, money changers had already been charging over 1,600 dinars per dollar; after the news it jumped past 1,700. In the northern city of Irbil, many exchange shops closed. A Baghdad clothing seller who imports from China said he will lose money: “People owe us in Iraqi dinars, and we owe people in China in dollars.”
stories.why_it_matters: This shows how a far-away war reaches ordinary wallets. Iraqi families who buy imported food, medicine and clothes will likely pay more. It is also a warning sign about how much the Iran war is straining oil-dependent economies in the region.
stories.camps: Government view: the change was needed “to meet the relevant financial, economic and monetary requirements” and close the gap with the street rate. Traders and shoppers: they fear losses and higher prices. Economists generally note devaluation can help a budget in the short term but can fuel inflation and hurt people with savings in dinars.
stories.image_alt: A currency exchanger counts bundles of Iraqi dinar banknotes at a street-side exchange in Baghdad on Oct. 7, 2026.

terms.explain: When a government makes its money worth less compared with other money.
The money used in Iraq.
A narrow sea passage near Iran that much of the world’s oil passes through.
How much of one money you get for another, like dinars per dollar.
A country’s main bank that manages its money and interest rates.

stories.headline: Microsoft unveils Nvidia-powered AI laptops and a Windows 11 update built to “sandbox” AI agents
stories.dek: The Surface Laptop Ultra starts around $2,600; a developer box starts near $6,000. Microsoft is even offering up to $1,000 off for trading in a MacBook Pro.
stories.caveman: At an event in San Francisco on Wednesday, Microsoft showed new Surface computers built on Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. The Surface Laptop Ultra comes in two base models, starting at about $2,600 and $3,700. There is also a desk machine for programmers, the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, starting at about $6,000. The big idea: run AI models right on your own computer instead of paying to use them in the cloud. Microsoft also showed a revamped Windows 11 with a feature called “Execution Containers.” Think of it as a fenced playpen: an AI “agent” (a program that can take actions for you, like opening files) works inside the fence so it can’t mess with everything else. CEO Satya Nadella said this will come to all Windows 11 users. He said a model alone “doesn’t do much”; you need memory and tools around it. Microsoft is clearly chasing developers who love Macs; it is offering up to $1,000 off if you trade in a MacBook Pro.
stories.why_it_matters: AI agents are moving from chat windows into the operating system, the base software of your computer. That could save time, but it also means AI gets closer to your files, passwords and accounts, so safety walls really matter.
stories.camps: Microsoft’s pitch: local AI is private and free to run, and containers keep agents safe. Skeptics’ points: these machines are very expensive, and letting AI agents control files raises big security and privacy questions that a sandbox may not fully solve. Rivals like Apple are also racing for the same developer crowd.
stories.image_alt: Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra.

terms.explain: An AI program that can take actions for you, like opening apps or editing files, not just chat.
A sealed-off space where a program can run without touching the rest of the computer.
A U.S. company that makes the chips most AI systems run on.
The base software that runs a computer, like Windows or macOS.
Running directly on your own computer or phone instead of on a company’s servers.

stories.headline: Watchdog says ChatGPT for Teens is an “unacceptable risk”; OpenAI pushes back on the testing
stories.dek: Common Sense Media found parent alerts often failed, crisis help fell short, and the bot still did kids’ homework.
stories.caveman: In August, OpenAI launched “ChatGPT for Teens,” a version with guardrails (safety rules) meant to help students learn. Common Sense Media, a U.S. nonprofit that rates apps and media for kids’ safety, tested it and on Wednesday called it an “unacceptable risk.” Their findings: it “doesn’t send alerts to parents when it should,” doesn’t give “the right help in crisis situations,” and “still does kids’ homework.” Tom Siegel of the group’s Youth AI Safety Institute said: “A teen can spend an hour talking about self-harm without their parent getting a single alert.” He said ChatGPT should be for adults only until OpenAI fixes this and proves it with independent tests. OpenAI disagreed. A spokesperson said the company is “deeply committed to teen safety” but does not believe the testing reflects how the safeguards work in real life. OpenAI said its parent alerts can take several hours to switch on for newly linked accounts. Common Sense answered that some test accounts were linked much longer and still got no alerts.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of teenagers use AI chatbots for school and for emotional support. If safety alerts don’t work, parents may feel safe when they shouldn’t. This fight is also shaping how lawmakers think about rules for AI and kids.
stories.camps: Common Sense Media: the protections “fall short of what the company promised,” and parents could get “false confidence.” OpenAI: the review’s methods were flawed, and AI can support teens’ learning and creativity with the right tools. Many child-safety experts say both sides agree on one thing: independent testing of these products is needed.
stories.image_alt: The OpenAI logo in an illustration.

terms.explain: Safety rules built into software to stop harmful uses.
An organization that does not exist to make money for owners.
When a person hurts themselves on purpose; a sign they need help.
Protections meant to prevent harm.
The U.S. company that makes ChatGPT.

stories.headline: FCC weighs letting more political robocalls, including AI voices, flood cellphones before the midterms
stories.dek: A right-leaning group asked for a waiver; the FCC’s only Democrat warns of “a tsunami of robocalls and misinformation.”
stories.caveman: A robocall is an automatic phone call that plays a recorded or computer voice. Right now, U.S. law bans most robocalls to cellphones unless you agreed to get them. The Club for Growth, a right-leaning political group, has asked the FCC (the government agency that oversees phones and TV) for a “waiver,” a special exception, so political groups can send robocalls with artificial or prerecorded voices without permission. The Republican-led FCC opened the idea for public comment and could decide as soon as late October, just before the November midterm elections. Why people worry: in 2024, New Hampshire voters got a fake robocall with an AI copy of President Joe Biden’s voice telling them not to vote in the primary. After that, the FCC ruled AI voice-cloning robocalls illegal. If this waiver passes, groups of all parties could use AI to call voters, and even have AI chatbots hold live conversations with them.
stories.why_it_matters: Midterms decide which party controls Congress for the last two years of President Trump’s term. Floods of AI calls in the final days could spread false information faster than anyone can check it, and land right on almost every voter’s phone.
stories.camps: Club for Growth: political speech deserves at least the same treatment as calls about package deliveries or doctor visits; the change could help reach voters in more languages and make polls more accurate. Critics: FCC commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat, said it would “supercharge” dark-money AI tricks; election-safety experts say it opens “a huge opportunity for abuse.” Critics also note the FCC has grown closely aligned with the president. The FCC did not comment.
stories.image_alt: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr testifies before a House subcommittee on Capitol Hill on Jan. 14, 2026.

terms.explain: An automatic phone call that plays a recorded or computer-made voice.
Federal Communications Commission, the U.S. agency that regulates phones, TV and radio.
An official exception to a rule.
U.S. elections held halfway through a president’s four-year term, for Congress and many state offices.
Using AI to copy a real person’s voice so it can say things they never said.
Political spending where the donors are hidden from the public.

stories.headline: Google opens a free website where anyone can check if a picture, video or audio clip was made with Google’s AI
stories.dek: The SynthID checker reads a hidden “watermark” that Google, OpenAI, Nvidia and others put into AI media.
stories.caveman: It is getting hard to tell real photos and videos from AI fakes. Google’s answer is SynthID, a hidden “watermark” it started adding in 2023. A watermark here is an invisible signal baked into the file, not a visible logo. Google’s AI tools, like Nano Banana (images), Veo (video), Lyria (music) and Gemini, all stamp their creations with it. OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao also support SynthID, and Apple is reportedly adding support soon. On Tuesday Google opened a website where anyone can upload a file to check for the watermark. It works with many formats: JPG, PNG and HEIC photos; MP4 and MOV videos; and MP3 and WAV audio. Before, only some journalists and researchers could test it. Google says people already make about 1 million checks a day through the Gemini app and Chrome.
stories.why_it_matters: Fake AI images and voices are used in scams, harassment and election lies. A free checking tool helps reporters and regular people. But it only catches content from tools that use SynthID.
stories.camps: Supporters: a shared watermark across big companies is a real step toward trust online. Limits critics point out: AI tools that don’t use SynthID (including many free, open ones) won’t be caught, so “no watermark found” does not prove something is real; watermarks may also be stripped or damaged; and one company running the checker gives it a lot of power.
stories.image_alt: The homepage of Google’s SynthID Detector website.

terms.explain: A hidden signal inside a file that shows where it came from.
Google’s system for hiding watermarks in AI-made images, video, audio and text.
Made by artificial intelligence instead of a camera or a person.

stories.headline: Russian missiles and drones kill at least 25 across Ukraine, including 5 children, in an attack Kyiv saw coming
stories.dek: Ukraine had warned of a “massive” strike; it hit on Putin’s 74th birthday. Ukraine is short of Patriot missiles because of the Iran war.
stories.caveman: Overnight into Wednesday, Russia fired missiles and drones at Kyiv and about a dozen other regions of Ukraine. At least 25 civilians died, including five children, and about 100 were hurt. The worst hit was an apartment block in Pryluky, in the northern Chernihiv region: 19 people died there, including the five children; three were 1 year old and one was 8. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned a day earlier that Russia was preparing a “massive” strike. Ukraine knew, but could not stop it all. Ukraine is searching the world for Patriot air-defense missiles, which are scarce because the Iran war is using them up. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it hit factories and storage sites for missiles and drones, plus ports and ships carrying military cargo. Ukraine has been hitting back at Russian oil refineries and depots with long-range drones; Zelenskyy said Ukraine hit two oil sites and a training ground in Russia.
stories.why_it_matters: The war is more than 4½ years old and stuck on the ground, so both sides are fighting a long-distance air war. That puts ordinary people in apartment buildings on the front line, and it shows how the Iran war drains weapons that Ukraine needs.
stories.camps: Ukraine and Europe: Zelenskyy called it the “gift” Putin gave himself for his birthday; EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it “a deliberate strategy of terror.” Russia: says it targets military industry, not civilians. U.S. senators are pushing the Trump administration to move faster on Russian sanctions. Independent checks of some battlefield claims were not possible.
stories.image_alt: Locals and rescuers carry an injured man from a residential building destroyed by a Russian missile in Pryluky, Ukraine, on Oct. 7, 2026.

terms.explain: A U.S.-made air-defense system that shoots down missiles and planes.
Weapons and radar used to stop missiles and drones from hitting targets.
People who are not soldiers.
Penalties, like trade bans, that countries use to pressure another country.
A factory that turns crude oil into fuel.

stories.headline: Three years after Oct. 7, Israel’s election on Oct. 27 is turning into a vote on Netanyahu
stories.dek: Opponents call his coalition “the massacre government”; Netanyahu says he led a “war of redemption.”
stories.caveman: On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas militants attacked southern Israel. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. Israel answered with a war in Gaza that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians, according to local health officials, and left Gaza in ruins. Now Israel holds its first national election since that day, on Oct. 27. Almost every poster and debate mentions Oct. 7. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who turns 77 soon, is the only top leader from that day still in office, after other security chiefs resigned. His main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief who leads the centrist Yashar party. Opponents across the spectrum want Netanyahu held responsible for the security failure. Netanyahu has rejected an official inquiry and blames security officials; he denies U.S. media reports that the UAE and Egypt warned him beforehand. Both main parties include grieving parents of people killed that day on their candidate lists.
stories.why_it_matters: This election decides who leads Israel on war, Gaza, Iran and relations with the world. Israel’s standing abroad has fallen sharply, several governments accuse it of genocide (which it rejects), and Netanyahu is wanted by the International Criminal Court.
stories.camps: Netanyahu’s side: he was let down by the military and led a dramatic comeback; “we didn’t collapse,” he told the U.N. Opponents: Eisenkot says the vote is “between taking responsibility and fleeing from responsibility.” A pollster at the Israel Democracy Institute says the whole country is “post-traumatic in a way.” Palestinians in Gaza, still living in ruins, have no vote in this election.
stories.image_alt: A man rides a bicycle past a TV ad showing Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan, Israel.

terms.explain: A Palestinian militant group that ruled Gaza and led the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
A group of political parties that join together to run a government.
An official independent investigation into what went wrong.
A court in The Hague that tries people for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
In the political middle, not strongly left or right.

stories.headline: Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports kill 3 as Yemen’s war reignites
stories.dek: Strikes hit Abha and Riyadh’s main airport; a Saudi-led offensive fights for Yemen’s Red Sea coast and a key shipping strait.
stories.caveman: The Houthis are an Iran-backed rebel group that controls much of Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s neighbor. On Wednesday, attacks on two Saudi airports, Abha and King Khalid International in the capital Riyadh, killed three people, and the Houthis took credit. In Abha, a Moroccan and an Algerian resident died and 28 people were hurt; in Riyadh a Sudanese man died and eight were hurt. Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, has put new cage-like fences around fuel tanks near the Riyadh airport. Behind this: last month the Houthis grabbed land along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow sea gate that about 12% of world trade passes through. Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces launched a big counterattack. Both sides now claim to control key places like the town of Dhubab, and AP could not verify either claim. The fighting broke a four-year truce.
stories.why_it_matters: Ships carrying goods between Asia and Europe pass the Bab el-Mandeb. Fighting there can raise shipping and fuel costs worldwide. For Yemenis, the U.N. says almost 1,000 people have died in the latest fighting and over 200,000 have been forced from their homes, with cholera and hunger rising.
stories.camps: Saudi-led coalition: promises “full operational support” until the Houthis are “eliminated,” with U.S. help including intelligence. Houthis: say they are hitting back at Saudi attacks on Yemeni cities and pledge support for Palestinians. A Washington think tank says the Houthis want to raise Saudi Arabia’s economic costs by hitting airports and oil sites. Aid groups warn civilians on both sides are paying the price.
stories.image_alt: A Houthi supporter carries a rifle at an armed tribal rally in Sanaa, Yemen, on Oct. 7, 2026.

terms.explain: An Iran-backed rebel group that controls Yemen’s capital and much of the north.
A narrow strait between Yemen and Africa that links the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
An agreement to stop fighting for a while.
Forced to leave home because of war or disaster.
A disease spread by dirty water that causes severe diarrhea and can kill quickly.

stories.headline: Brazil’s runoff may be decided by people who like neither Lula nor Bolsonaro
stories.dek: Over 33 million people (21%) skipped the first round, the most since 1998; nearly 6 million voted blank or spoiled.
stories.caveman: Brazil’s presidential election goes to a second round on Oct. 25. It is left-leaning President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against right-wing Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for planning a coup. In the first round on Sunday, Bolsonaro got about 2 million more votes than Lula, and the next three finishers were all on the right. But a huge group did not pick either. Voting is mandatory in Brazil for literate citizens 18 to 70 (skipping brings a small fine), yet more than 33 million people, 21% of voters, stayed home, the highest first-round no-show since 1998. Nearly 6 million more cast blank or spoiled ballots. Before the first round, the Datafolha poll found about 11% undecided, versus just 2% at this point in 2022. A 19-year-old theater student told AP she distrusts both: one side mixes religion and politics, the other is tied to corruption. A 21-year-old with three part-time jobs leans Lula but says, “things are more expensive.”
stories.why_it_matters: Brazil is Latin America’s biggest country and home to most of the Amazon rainforest. Who wins will shape climate policy, democracy and relations with the U.S. and China.
stories.camps: Bolsonaro’s edge: more first-round votes and endorsements from right-wing rivals. Lula’s hope: turn out voters who stayed home. Many voters: worn out by polarization; one political scientist says people forget “the higher percentage of people who don’t like this fight.” Both candidates face doubts over corruption: Flávio Bolsonaro is under investigation, and Lula was jailed for 19 months on charges that were later annulled.
stories.image_alt: People walk past campaign flags of President Lula and challenger Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro in Rio de Janeiro on Oct. 5, 2026.

terms.explain: A second-round vote between the top two candidates when no one wins a majority.
Choosing not to vote.
A rule that citizens must vote, often with a small fine if they don’t.
When a society splits into two hostile camps.
An illegal grab of government power, often with force.

stories.headline: Oprah picks a 28-year-old’s debut, “Hungered,” about a 12-year-old girl growing up unhoused
stories.dek: Amanda Rizkalla’s novel came out in May; landing in Oprah’s Book Club usually sends a book soaring.
stories.caveman: Oprah Winfrey has run her famous book club for 30 years, and a pick can turn an unknown writer into a bestseller almost overnight. Her new choice is “Hungered” by Amanda Rizkalla, a first novel that came out in May. It follows a 12-year-old girl trying to find herself amid poverty and family trouble. Winfrey called it a “riveting novel” about “families who live outside the margins, living unhoused” and “their hopes, dreams, and the perseverance” to keep going. Rizkalla is 28. She grew up in Los Angeles, now lives in the Bay Area, studied at Stanford and earned a creative-writing master’s (MFA) at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. She said she was “so stunned I could hardly believe it was real.” Her talk with Oprah is on Winfrey’s YouTube channel and podcast.
stories.why_it_matters: Who’s hot: a young debut author writing about homelessness, a crisis that touches many U.S. cities, especially in California. An Oprah pick can put a story about poor families in front of millions of readers who might never pick it up otherwise.
stories.camps: Fans of the club: Oprah has a long record of lifting new and diverse voices. Common critique of celebrity book clubs: one person’s taste gets huge power over what sells, while many strong books get no spotlight. Readers who have lived without housing also often ask that such stories be told with care and not as “poverty tourism.”
stories.image_alt: The cover of “Hungered” by Amanda Rizkalla.

terms.explain: A writer’s first published book.
Without a stable home; another word for homeless.
A group that reads and discusses the same book; Oprah’s is the most famous in the U.S.
Master of Fine Arts, a graduate degree many fiction writers earn.

stories.headline: Barbara Kingsolver’s “Partita,” her first novel since the Pulitzer-winning “Demon Copperhead,” is about a pianist, art and class
stories.dek: Kingsolver, who has a condition that bends her fingers, writes about bodies that fail, suicide and why we need art.
stories.caveman: Barbara Kingsolver is one of America’s best-known novelists. Her last book, “Demon Copperhead,” a retelling of Dickens’ “David Copperfield” set in Appalachia during the opioid crisis, won the Pulitzer Prize. Her new novel, “Partita,” her 19th, is out this week. It follows Livia, a serious classical pianist whose love of music clashes with a first, all-consuming romance. Kingsolver plays piano herself, but she has Dupuytren’s contracture, an inherited condition that slowly pulls her fingers into a fist; she needs surgery every couple of years. That struggle shaped the book. In an interview at her home in southwestern Virginia, she said the novel asks “why do we need art?” at a time of cuts “from the NEA all the way down to second grade music classes.” The book also deals with suicide; she said she has lost four people close to her that way. She also spoke up for Appalachia: outsiders “think we’re stupid,” she said, when the region’s poverty comes from “hundreds of years of exploitation” by coal and other industries.
stories.why_it_matters: Who’s hot: Kingsolver after a Pulitzer is a major literary event of the fall. Her talk about class barriers to the arts and about the rural South pushes back on easy stereotypes of “flyover country.”
stories.camps: Admirers: she gives working-class and rural people complex, dignified stories, and links personal pain to big social questions. Points some readers debate: “Partita” is a tighter, more personal book than the sweeping “Demon Copperhead,” and some critics prefer her big social novels. Kingsolver herself credits Appalachian writers like Wendell Berry, Bobbie Ann Mason and Silas House.
stories.image_alt: Artwork showing Barbara Kingsolver’s name and the title “Partita.”

terms.explain: A top U.S. award for books, journalism and music.
A mountain region in the eastern U.S., including parts of Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia.
National Endowment for the Arts, a U.S. government agency that funds the arts.
A piece of classical music made of several short parts.
The wave of addiction and overdose deaths from painkillers and drugs like fentanyl.

stories.headline: Lydia Millet’s “Fair Ones” is a “double novel” about two Brooklyn friends after a murder
stories.dek: The first half is told by Mara right after their friend Claire is killed; the second, by Jen a year later.
stories.caveman: Lydia Millet is a respected American novelist known for sharp, darkly funny books. Her new novel, “Fair Ones,” is really two short novels in one, called “Fair” and “Ones.” Two Brooklyn women in their forties, Mara and Jen, lose their longtime friend Claire, who is murdered. In “Fair,” Mara tells the story just after the killing. In “Ones,” Jen picks it up a year later. The two women stumble through shock, numbness, anger, regret and depression, spend time with others who knew Claire, and try to figure out how she died. Lit Hub calls it “an exquisite rendering” of grief that lingers. Millet said she wanted to test herself: could she write something realistic, “mostly dialogue,” about a small group of people, “and not be bored” writing it? She likes that the word “fair” can mean beautiful, just, or merely so-so.
stories.why_it_matters: Who’s hot: Millet, who was a National Book Award finalist before, is among the big literary names with new books this fall, next to Kingsolver and Patricia Lockwood. Books about grief and friendship between women are drawing a lot of readers right now.
stories.camps: Fans: praise her sharp dialogue, quick pacing and sardonic edge. Possible drawbacks for some readers: a story told mostly through talk and with two narrators can feel slow if you want a twisty crime plot; this is a book about grief, not a whodunit.
stories.image_alt: Portrait of novelist Lydia Millet.

terms.explain: One book made of two linked short novels.
The character who tells the story.
Grimly mocking or darkly funny.
Fiction that shows everyday life as it is, without fantasy.

stories.headline: Netflix’s new “East of Eden” brings Steinbeck back, with Florence Pugh as the novel’s famous villain
stories.dek: Zoe Kazan, granddaughter of the director of the 1955 James Dean film, made the roughly seven-hour series.
stories.caveman: “East of Eden” is John Steinbeck’s big 1952 novel about several generations of the Trask family in California, from the Civil War to World War I. It is built around two brothers who echo Cain and Abel from the Bible, and around a scary, manipulative woman named Cathy. Steinbeck’s big question: are we born good or bad, or can we choose? Many Americans read it in school or saw the 1955 movie with James Dean, which only used the last part of the book. Now Netflix has a new miniseries of about seven hours, made by Zoe Kazan, granddaughter of that film’s director, Elia Kazan. NPR critics say Florence Pugh gives a “fantastic” performance as Cathy and call the series a fresh retelling for new audiences. NPR’s TV critic notes it mostly cuts the Irish American Hamilton family from the book, but praises Hoon Lee as Lee, the family’s Chinese caretaker, and Martha Plimpton.
stories.why_it_matters: Who’s hot: classic American novels are getting new life on streaming, sending new readers back to the book. Steinbeck’s question about choice versus fate still feels timely.
stories.camps: Praise: NPR says Pugh “fills” the spotlight and the series hammers home Steinbeck’s main theme. Criticism: it is not more complete than the 1981 TV version because it drops the Hamiltons, and it adds lots of sex and nudity that some viewers may find heavy. Book purists usually say: read the novel too.
stories.image_alt: Florence Pugh in Netflix’s “East of Eden.”

terms.explain: A TV series with a fixed, small number of episodes that tells one complete story.
A new version of a story made for a different form, like a book turned into a show.
Brothers in the Bible; Cain kills Abel out of jealousy.
A Nobel Prize-winning American writer of “The Grapes of Wrath” and “East of Eden.”

stories.headline: A lab worker’s death in Siberia sparks fears of pneumonic plague; WHO asks Russia for more answers
stories.dek: The 28-year-old worked at an anti-plague institute; Russia says no plague was found in contacts, but the WHO says it “does not yet have the full picture.”
stories.caveman: On Oct. 2 a 28-year-old woman who worked at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk, in Siberia, died in a hospital nearby. Early unconfirmed reports said she may have caught pneumonic plague after an accidental lab exposure. Russian officials say she died of what first looked like a “typical” respiratory virus and that no recent plague cases were found. Still, the local hospital was put under quarantine, and Russia told the World Health Organization (WHO) that 200 contacts were quarantined. Russia says tests found no dangerous germs in any contacts. Simple background: plague is caused by the same germ that caused the Black Death in the 1300s, which killed 30% to 50% of people in parts of Europe. Bubonic plague comes from flea bites. Pneumonic plague infects the lungs and spreads person to person by coughing. It can kill fast if untreated, but antibiotics cure it if caught early. WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said it is also checking reports of a second worker.
stories.why_it_matters: When a dangerous germ might have escaped a lab, the world needs fast, honest information. The case brings back memories of COVID-19 and questions about lab safety. The WHO says the risk outside Russia is “very low.”
stories.camps: WHO: Russia has answered questions, but more data is needed on lab tests and contacts before a full risk check. Russia: says the situation is “stable,” and the Kremlin told people to trust official statements over “rumors or speculation.” President Trump said he has a call scheduled with Putin about it. Health experts note plague still appears every year in parts of Africa and the U.S., and it is treatable.
stories.image_alt: Electric scooters parked next to the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, Russia, on Oct. 7, 2026.

terms.explain: A lung form of plague that spreads between people through coughing.
The flea-bite form of plague that causes painful swollen lumps.
Keeping possibly sick people apart so a disease doesn’t spread.
World Health Organization, the U.N. agency for global health.
Medicines that kill bacteria.
A plague pandemic in the 1300s that killed a huge share of people in Europe, Asia and Africa.

stories.headline: Congo’s Ebola outbreak creates new hot spots as responders call the effort “chaotic”
stories.dek: Over 4,000 dead and 8,500 cases, the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record; most new cases come from people nobody was tracking.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a virus that causes severe bleeding and often death. It spreads through body fluids, including when people wash or touch the bodies of those who died. Since May, eastern Congo has had its deadliest Ebola outbreak ever: more than 8,500 cases and over 4,000 deaths. This strain, Bundibugyo, has no approved vaccine or treatment. Africa CDC head Dr. Jean Kaseya told AP that more than 70% of new cases come from people who were not on any list of known contacts, and at least 60% of deaths happen outside treatment centers. Only 23% of contacts have been traced. North Kivu province, battered by armed conflict, is now the center: about 40% of new cases, up from 24% at the end of August. There, 58% of confirmed patients die. A doctors’ group, MSF, calls the response “chaotic.” Some residents don’t believe the disease is real, and families sometimes hold quick funerals or refuse tests. On Tuesday Kenya reported its first case, a man from Congo who died.
stories.why_it_matters: Diseases do not stop at borders; Kenya’s case shows the risk of spread. The outbreak also shows how war, distrust and poverty make health emergencies worse, and how cuts in global health aid can leave gaps.
stories.camps: Africa CDC: wants a “village-centered approach,” with local leaders helping with tracing, safe burials and isolation. MSF: local health workers face an awful choice between sending sick neighbors home or risking their own lives. WHO: treatment centers lack staff and supplies. Researchers note that mistrust of outsiders, after years of conflict, is a major barrier.
stories.image_alt: A health worker in protective clothing is disinfected inside an Ebola treatment center in Beni, North Kivu, Congo, on Sept. 26, 2026.

terms.explain: A deadly virus that spreads through body fluids and causes fever and bleeding.
Finding everyone a sick person was near so they can be checked and kept apart.
The African Union’s public health agency.
Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders), a medical aid group.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in one area.

stories.headline: Maricarmen, the 87-year-old whose eviction shook Spain, dies in hospital before she could go home
stories.dek: Her removal from her home of seven decades sparked nationwide housing protests; unions plan a general strike next month.
stories.caveman: María del Carmen Abascal, known as “Maricarmen,” lived in the same Madrid apartment for about 70 years. Her parents died there. On Sept. 23 police cordoned off the street and she, using a wheelchair, was carried out on a stretcher. A real estate company had evicted her so it could rent the place for much more money. TV images of the eviction set off protests in Madrid and across Spain. Under huge public pressure, the company backed down and agreed to let her return. But on Wednesday she died in the hospital. Her lawyer did not give a cause of death. Protesters near Parliament chanted, “Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!” In Puerta del Sol square they held a minute of silence. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wrote: “Rest in peace.” Background: average rent in Spain has almost doubled in 10 years, and about a quarter of renters spend some 40% of their income on rent and bills, compared with an EU average of 18% of renters.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing costs are squeezing people in many countries, including Taiwan. Maricarmen’s case made a huge issue personal. It has pushed Spain into a political crisis: Sánchez called an early election for Nov. 29 after Parliament blocked emergency housing measures.
stories.camps: Tenants’ union: “this solution came too late,” calling it “an entirely avoidable situation.” Protesters: blame landlords and the system; one said “they have killed her.” Government: approved 21 urgent housing measures and wants voters to back them. Property owners and conservative parties usually argue that rent limits and tough rules scare off investors and shrink the supply of homes. The cause of death has not been made public.
stories.image_alt: Protesters gather in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square after the death of María del Carmen Abascal on Oct. 7, 2026.

terms.explain: Forcing a tenant to leave their home, often with police help.
A group of renters who organize to defend their rights.
When workers across many jobs stop work at the same time to protest.
An election called earlier than planned.

stories.headline: Satellite photos show Israel has erased whole Gaza towns, and demolitions kept going after the ceasefire
stories.dek: Rafah, once home to a quarter million people, is gone; at least 50 Israeli military outposts now dot the Israeli-held part of Gaza.
stories.caveman: AP studied satellite pictures of Gaza from a company called Planet Labs. They show that the southern city of Rafah, which once had about 250,000 people, has been flattened. Other towns, like Bani Suheila, were razed (knocked to the ground) with bulldozers and explosives, and in some places the rubble was cleared away. That demolition kept going even after the Israel-Hamas ceasefire a year ago. Gaza’s 2 million Palestinians are now squeezed into about 40% of the territory; Israel’s army controls the rest. At least 50 Israeli military outposts sit in that area, 18 built since the ceasefire. More than 1 in 10 people from Gaza’s prewar population has been killed or wounded. AP met Najwa Abu Eita, a former hairdresser who lost her 7-year-old daughter and one eye in a 2024 strike and now lives in a tent by her ruined home. Her 4-year-old told her, “Momma, I’ll give you one of my eyes.”
stories.why_it_matters: Where people can return, rebuild or live depends on what is left standing. The scale of destruction also matters for international law and for any future peace plan.
stories.camps: Israel’s military: says it destroys buildings so Hamas can’t use them or its tunnels, and that it targets militants who hide among civilians; it rejects genocide accusations. A U.N.-appointed expert: said in February that the destruction is “unprecedented” in modern war and could be a crime against humanity or reach genocide. Palestinians: say almost daily strikes still kill women and children despite the ceasefire.
stories.image_alt: Palestinians walk along a street lined with destroyed buildings in Gaza City on Oct. 6, 2026.

terms.explain: Pictures of the ground taken from space.
An agreement to stop fighting.
To completely destroy a building or town.
A small military base in an area controlled by an army.
A grave crime, like mass killing or forced displacement, aimed at civilians on a large scale.
Acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part.
